Text:
‎{{c1::أب}}

Transliteration: {{c1::ab}}

{{c2::father}} — the formal word — and the first word she ever had you write
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — ab

Why: alif + baa. The word opens on a glottal stop, so the alif carries a hamza on top.

Distinguish: ab is the formal word for father; baaba is what a child calls him.

Ex: she taught it as the payoff of the hamza lesson — "and you learned your first word, ab."

Pitfall: she called this REQUIRED.

Text:

Transliteration: {{c1::abii}}

{{c2::my father}} — ab with the ending that means "my"

Text: A word that begins with a glottal stop has to be written {{c1::with a hamza on its alif}} — above the alif for a and u, below it for i. The one word that takes no hamza at all is the definite article {{c2::al-}}.
Back Extra:
Why: she taught it as a listening test — if you hear a word start with a glottal stop, think hamza straight away.

Ex: ab and umm both take the hamza; al- does not.

Pitfall: the alif still sounds the same either way — the hamza is about how it is written, not how it is said.
verified_against: lecture recording
verified_by: mlx-whisper english pass
audio_source: NO AUDIO — concept card, nothing to pronounce.

Text: The NAME of a letter ends in a hamza that the letter itself does not have — so baa, taa and thaa are written {{c1::باء · تاء · ثاء}}, not {{c2::با · تا · ثا}}.
Back Extra:
Why: she wrote the names beside the letters on the board and stopped to point the hamza out.

Pitfall: she also warned not to confuse the mark hamza with the personal name Hamza, which has a Haa.

Ex: waaw and yaa follow the same pattern — واو and ياء.

audio_source: NO AUDIO — concept card, nothing to pronounce.

Text: The -uu that turns a verb plural — as in tuubuu — is called {{c1::waaw al-jamaaca}}, literally {{c2::the waaw of the group}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: tub is "repent" to one person; tuubuu is "repent" to a group.

Pitfall: this is one plural pattern, not the rule. She called Arabic plurals "very inconsistent" and pushed broken plurals to 102.
